pm.label: Product Management
pm.headline: Reviewers scan first for the product outcome you moved, the decision you personally made to move it, and the scope behind it (users, revenue, teams).
pm.summary_formula: [Product manager] with [N years] in [domain or product type] who [signature outcome pattern, e.g. takes products from 0 to 1 or grows self-serve revenue]; [one proof point with a number or placeholder]. Keep one positioning; no adjectives like passionate or results-driven.

bullet_formulas.name: Outcome by Decision (XYZ)
bullet_formulas.template: [Moved metric] from [baseline] to [result] in [timeframe] by [decision you made] and [how it was executed].
bullet_formulas.when: Default for any bullet where a metric moved; makes the PM's own call separable from the team's build.

bullet_formulas.name: Launch and Traction
bullet_formulas.template: Launched [product or feature] for [audience or segment], reaching [adoption or revenue] within [timeframe] by [scoping or sequencing decision].
bullet_formulas.when: 0-to-1 work or major launches where adoption or revenue after launch is the proof.

bullet_formulas.name: Insight to Bet
bullet_formulas.template: [Discovery method and volume] revealed [insight], leading to [decision or reframed roadmap], which [result].
bullet_formulas.when: Discovery, research or data-insight stories; the insight must change what was built.

bullet_formulas.name: Cut and Redirect
bullet_formulas.template: [Cut, killed or deprioritized] [work] after [evidence], redirecting [capacity] to [new priority], which [result].
bullet_formulas.when: Prioritization and judgment stories, including killed projects and roadmap trade-offs.

skills.name: 0-to-1 Product Launch
skills.definition: Taking a new product or feature from idea to market and proving it found real usage.
metrics: accounts or users reached in first 30 to 90 days
activation rate of the launch cohort
revenue or ARR from the new product
skills.example: Launched self-serve invoicing for SMB customers 10 weeks after kickoff, reaching 1,800 paying accounts and $410K ARR in two quarters by scoping the MVP to the 3 highest-volume workflows.

skills.name: Growth and Adoption
skills.definition: Getting more of the right users to discover, activate and reach first value.
skills.example: Raised new-user activation from 31% to 44% in one quarter by replacing a 9-step setup wizard with a guided first project, adding about 2,600 activated accounts per month.

skills.name: Monetization and Pricing
skills.definition: Turning product value into revenue through pricing, packaging, upsell and conversion decisions.
skills.example: Repackaged 3 plans into usage-based tiers after 22 willingness-to-pay interviews, raising free-to-paid conversion from 3.1% to 4.0% and ARPU 12% with flat churn over 2 quarters.

skills.name: Retention and Engagement
skills.definition: Keeping users who already activated coming back, and keeping customers renewing.
skills.example: Cut monthly logo churn from 2.8% to 2.1% for mid-market accounts by prioritizing bulk edit and usage alerts, the top 2 drivers found in a cancellation analysis of 340 accounts.

skills.name: User Research and Discovery
skills.definition: Finding the right problem to solve through interviews, prototypes and evidence before committing engineering time.
metrics: interviews or field sessions tied to a decision
engineering time saved by killing weak ideas
skills.example: Interviewed 28 warehouse managers and tested 3 clickable prototypes, reframing the roadmap from reporting to exception alerts; the alerts beta reached 63% weekly use among pilot accounts.

skills.name: Experimentation
skills.definition: Running controlled tests to decide what ships, and acting on the results, including the negative ones.
metrics: revenue or conversion impact of winners
skills.example: Ran 14 checkout A/B tests over 2 quarters with design and data science, shipping 5 winners that raised mobile conversion from 2.3% to 2.9%, about $1.2M in annualized GMV.

skills.name: Prioritization and Roadmap
skills.definition: Deciding what the team builds and what it does not, and sequencing work toward a strategy.
metrics: share of capacity moved to top bets
items cut or deferred with rationale
time to market for the top priority
skills.example: Cut 6 of 15 committed roadmap items after sizing each against renewal risk, shifting 40% of team capacity to SSO and audit logs, which unblocked $2.3M in stalled enterprise renewals.

skills.name: Product Analytics
skills.definition: Defining the metrics a product is judged on and reading them well enough to change a decision.
metrics: north star metric defined and adopted
skills.example: Defined a weekly-active-projects north star and instrumented 40 events, finding 58% of trials never invited a teammate; the invite-first flow built in response lifted trial conversion 19%.

skills.name: Cross-Functional Leadership
skills.definition: Aligning engineering, design, sales, legal and support around one plan without formal authority.
skills.example: Aligned 5 teams across engineering, legal, sales and support on a phased EU data-residency launch, shipping on the committed date and retaining 11 enterprise accounts worth $3.4M ARR.

skills.name: Platform and API Products
skills.definition: Framing technical or internal products by the value they unlock for developers, partners or other teams.
skills.example: Productized an internal payments service into a public API with 3 partner pilots, cutting partner integration time from 6 weeks to 5 days and reaching 140 live integrations within a year.

skills.name: AI Product Development
skills.definition: Shipping AI or LLM features that solve a real user problem with measured quality, cost and trust.
skills.example: Launched an LLM support assistant gated by a 400-case eval set, resolving 34% of tier-1 tickets without escalation and cutting median first response from 4 hours to 2 minutes.

skills.name: Product Quality and UX
skills.definition: Improving how usable, fast and dependable the product feels, measured by customer experience outcomes.
metrics: error rate in a key flow
skills.example: Redesigned bulk upload after mapping the top 5 error paths with design, cutting median onboarding from 9 days to 3 and import-related support tickets 46% in one quarter.

examples: activation rate from X% to Y%
feature adoption as % of eligible users
lift on primary metric with test length
interviews or prototype tests tied to a decision
ideas killed before build and engineering time saved
engineers and designers on the team

avoid: Duty statements: Responsible for, Owned the roadmap for, In charge of
Worked with or Collaborated with engineering and design, with no outcome or decision
Helped, Assisted, Supported: hides what the PM actually decided
Rituals as achievements: ran standups, sprint planning, backlog grooming, wrote PRDs
Output as outcome: shipped 12 features, delivered 90% of the roadmap
Bare percentages with no baseline, timeframe or scope (increased engagement 30%)
Discovery volume with no decision (conducted 50 customer interviews)
Tool lists inside bullets (Jira, Figma, Amplitude) unless the posting requires a tool
Taking sole credit for a team result, or hiding your role behind we
Filler adjectives: successfully, various, key, strategic, cutting-edge

seniority.entry: Show shipped scope you owned end to end, even if small, plus evidence of discovery and data skills; internships, side products and technical projects count when they have real users or measured results.
seniority.mid: Own a feature area and prove you moved its core metric; each bullet should show a decision you made, not just a launch you took part in.
seniority.senior: Show strategy across a product area: multi-quarter bets, what you chose not to do, revenue or retention at scale, and alignment of teams outside your own.
seniority.staff_or_lead: Show portfolio or org-level impact: strategy adopted by leadership, new lines of business, PMs hired or coached, and planning or metrics mechanisms other teams now run on.

structure.bullets_per_role: 3 to 5 for the current or most relevant role, 2 to 3 for older roles, 1 to 2 for roles more than about 8 years back or unrelated.
structure.ordering: Strongest outcome first in every role. Aim for a mix: one launch or bet, one metric-moving optimization, one discovery or prioritization decision, one cross-functional or scale bullet. Reorder to mirror the posting's priorities.
structure.length: One page under about 10 years of experience. Each bullet is one sentence, 1 to 2 lines, under about 230 characters.
structure.skills_section: Short and specific: product methods (experimentation, discovery, pricing), domain (B2B SaaS, payments, marketplaces) and technical fluency (SQL, analytics tools, APIs, AI/LLM). No soft skills; prove those in bullets.
structure.summary: Optional. 1 to 2 lines with one positioning: domain, product type and one signature proof point. Most useful for career switchers and senior PMs.

story_types.name: 0-to-1 Launch
story_types.proves: Can find a new opportunity, scope an MVP and get real adoption.
story_types.example: Launched a contractor payouts product from concept to general availability in 5 months, reaching 900 businesses and $28M in monthly payment volume by month six.

story_types.name: Metric-Moving Optimization
story_types.proves: Can move a core metric in an existing product.
story_types.example: Lifted trial-to-paid conversion from 9% to 12% in one quarter by surfacing pricing during onboarding and adding a usage-based trial extension.

story_types.name: Discovery-Driven Bet
story_types.proves: Starts from evidence about users, not opinions.
story_types.example: Shadowed 15 dispatchers and found 40% of their day went to rescheduling, leading to an auto-reschedule feature now used on 70% of eligible jobs.

story_types.name: Kill or Cut Decision
story_types.proves: Has the judgment to stop work that will not pay off.
story_types.example: Killed a planned marketplace after a 6-week concierge test showed 4% repeat use, moving 5 engineers to retention work that cut monthly churn 0.6 points.

story_types.name: Experiment-Led Learning
story_types.proves: Uses tests to decide and acts on negative results.
story_types.example: Ran a 3-arm pricing page test that disproved the annual-discount hypothesis, avoiding a change modeled to cost $250K a year in monthly-plan revenue.

story_types.name: Enterprise Unblock
story_types.proves: Connects product work directly to B2B revenue.
story_types.example: Shipped role-based permissions in 8 weeks after mapping blockers across 20 lost deals, helping close 7 enterprise contracts worth $1.9M ARR within two quarters.

story_types.name: Platform as Business Value
story_types.proves: Frames technical or internal work by what it unlocks.
story_types.example: Led a shared notifications platform adopted by 6 product teams, cutting time to add a new notification from 3 weeks to 2 days and duplicate alerts 35%.

story_types.name: Cross-Team Alignment
story_types.proves: Leads without authority across functions and teams.
story_types.example: Aligned 4 product teams and sales on one account model, resolving 3 conflicting roadmaps and enabling a multi-product bundle that drove $2.1M in new bookings.

story_types.name: Responsible AI Launch
story_types.proves: Can ship AI with quality, cost and trust guardrails.
story_types.example: Shipped AI meeting summaries behind a 250-sample eval and user feedback loop, reaching 41% weekly use among eligible teams with under 2% flagged inaccurate.

story_types.name: Mechanism That Outlasted You
story_types.proves: Builds durable practices that scale beyond one launch.
story_types.example: Created a launch-readiness review and metrics template adopted by 9 PMs, cutting post-launch critical bugs 50% over the following 3 quarters.

rewrites.weak: Responsible for the onboarding experience.
rewrites.strong: Cut median onboarding from 9 days to 3 by replacing manual CSV setup with a guided import, reducing setup-related support tickets 40% in one quarter.
rewrites.move: Duty to outcome: named the metric, the baseline and the product decision that moved it.

rewrites.weak: Worked with engineering and design to launch a new mobile app.
rewrites.strong: Launched the first mobile app for field technicians, reaching 12K weekly users in 90 days by scoping v1 to offline job checklists, the top need from 30 ride-alongs.
rewrites.move: Replaced worked with by the PM's own scoping decision and added adoption proof.

rewrites.weak: Managed the product roadmap and ran sprint planning.
rewrites.strong: Reprioritized a 2-quarter roadmap around renewal risk, cutting 4 committed features to ship SSO first, which unblocked $1.8M in delayed enterprise renewals.
rewrites.move: Ritual to decision: showed what was cut, why, and the business result.

rewrites.weak: Increased engagement by 30%.
rewrites.strong: Raised weekly use of saved reports from 18% to 24% of accounts in one quarter by adding scheduled email delivery, validated in a 4-week A/B test.
rewrites.move: Defined the metric and added baseline, timeframe, cause and evidence.

rewrites.weak: Conducted 50 customer interviews to understand user needs.
rewrites.strong: Ran 50 interviews with finance admins showing approvals, not reporting, drove month-end delays; refocused the roadmap and the approvals beta cut close time by 2 days.
rewrites.move: Discovery to decision: tied research to what changed and the measured result.

rewrites.weak: Leveraged AI to improve customer support using GPT-4 and LangChain.
rewrites.strong: Launched an AI reply assistant for 60 support agents after a 300-ticket eval, cutting average handle time from 11 to 7 minutes with no drop in CSAT.
rewrites.move: Dropped tool names and buzzwords; led with the user outcome and a quality guardrail.

questions.q: Why do you want to work on [company]'s product, and what would you change or build first?
What about our customers or market makes you a strong fit for this PM role?
Tell us about the product launch you are proudest of and how you measured its success.
What is the biggest product mistake you have made, and what did you change afterward?
How do you decide what not to build? Describe a feature or project you cut or killed.
Walk us through how you discovered a customer problem and validated it before building.
Describe a time data contradicted your intuition about a product decision. What did you do?
Tell us about a time you aligned engineering, design and go-to-market teams that disagreed.
Describe a decision you made with incomplete information. How did it turn out?
How do you use AI tools in your day-to-day product work, and where have they changed how you work?
Describe an AI or LLM feature you shipped or would ship here. How would you measure quality and decide it is ready to launch?

review_notes: Kept the baseline plus timeframe rule but relaxed it: when baselines are confidential, a relative change plus scope (users, revenue, segment) is acceptable. The notes stated it as absolute.
Removed % of roadmap shipped and time-to-market as success metrics. They measure output, not outcome; they now appear only as supporting context.
Demoted NPS and CSAT to secondary metrics because attribution to one PM's work is weak and screeners know it.

The notes called a discovery bullet nearly expected, based on one hiring-manager panel. Reframed as strongly recommended, and only when the research changed a decision; interview counts alone are a weak pattern.
Added an AI Product Development skill with eval, deflection and cost metrics. The notes treated AI only as an interview topic, but AI feature work is now a common PM bullet.
Raised current-role bullets from 3 to 4 to a range of 3 to 5. Most guidance and real PM resumes use 4 to 5 for the current role and fewer for older roles.

Dropped the per-company stereotypes (Meta speed, Apple craft, etc.) from the spec. They are secondhand generalizations, and the application questions attributed to Stripe were not verified. Tailoring should come from the job description itself.
Added Platform and API Products so technical PM roles are covered, framed by what the platform unlocks rather than how it works.
Separated PM metrics from engineering and BizOps metrics: PM owns adoption, conversion, retention and monetization; latency or cost savings appear only when tied to a user or revenue result.
pm.prompt_rules: PM bullets. Formula: [outcome metric, baseline to result, timeframe] by [decision the candidate made] and [how it was executed]. Lead with the product outcome (adoption, activation, conversion, revenue, retention, churn) or with the decision itself (launched, cut, prioritized, reframed). Make the candidate's own call visible: what they chose, cut, tested or sequenced, separate from what the team built. Metrics that count: users or accounts adopting, activation, conversion, ARR or ARPU, churn or NRR, experiment lift, time to value, tickets deflected. Discovery counts only when tied to the decision it changed. Shipped features, roadmap % and sprints are outputs, not outcomes. Add scope where real: users, revenue, segments, teams aligned. No tool names unless the job description requires them. Past tense for past work; present tense only for ongoing current-role work. One sentence, 1 to 2 lines, under 230 characters, no first-person pronouns. Never invent numbers; if a number is missing write a [bracketed placeholder] such as [X%] or [N accounts]. Banned: responsible for, worked on, worked with, helped, assisted, participated in, managed the roadmap, successfully, various, leveraged, utilized, drove synergies. No em dashes.

swe.label: Software Engineering
swe.headline: Reviewers scan first for what you built, at what scale, how much better it made the system (latency, reliability, cost, velocity), and whether your stack matches theirs.
swe.summary_formula: [Level] [specialty, e.g. backend or full-stack] engineer with [N years] building [system type] at [scale, e.g. requests/day or users]; [one proof point with a number or placeholder]. Core stack: [3 to 5 technologies from the posting that you actually use]. Omit for new grads unless switching fields.

bullet_formulas.name: Impact First (XYZ)
bullet_formulas.template: [Improved engineering metric] from [before] to [after] [at scale] by [technical change you made], using [technologies].
bullet_formulas.when: Default for performance, reliability, cost and velocity work with before/after numbers.

bullet_formulas.name: Build and Adoption
bullet_formulas.template: Built [system or feature] that [does what] for [users, teams or traffic], [adoption or business result], using [technologies].
bullet_formulas.when: New services, features or internal tools where usage or enablement is the proof.

bullet_formulas.name: Problem, Fix, Result
bullet_formulas.template: Diagnosed [failure or bottleneck] in [system], [fix you designed], [measured result and recurrence], using [technologies].
bullet_formulas.when: Incidents, debugging, hardening and migrations where the risk removed is the story.

bullet_formulas.name: Lead Through Others
bullet_formulas.template: [Authored, led or standardized] [design, RFC, migration] across [N engineers, teams or services], [outcome for those teams].
bullet_formulas.when: Senior and staff bullets where impact flows through other engineers.

skills.name: System Design and Scale
skills.definition: Choosing the architecture and data flow for a system so it keeps working as traffic, data and teams grow.
metrics: requests per second or events per day
skills.example: Re-architected order ingestion from synchronous calls to an event-driven pipeline, raising peak throughput from 1.2K to 9K orders/sec over the holidays with zero dropped events, using Kafka and Go.

skills.name: Performance Optimization
skills.definition: Profiling an existing code path, query or service and making it measurably faster or lighter without redesigning it.
skills.example: Cut search API p99 latency from 1.8s to 220ms across 40M listings by profiling hot paths, adding a read-through cache and removing 3 N+1 queries, using Redis and PostgreSQL.

skills.name: Reliability & Observability
skills.definition: Keeping systems available and making failures fast to detect, diagnose and recover from.
skills.example: Raised payments API availability from 99.5% to 99.95% by adding idempotent retries and a circuit breaker for an unstable provider, cutting Sev-2 incidents from 6 to 1 per month, using Go.

skills.name: Infrastructure and Cost
skills.definition: Running cloud infrastructure as code and keeping spend tied to real usage.
metrics: cost per request or per tenant
skills.example: Cut annual cloud spend $310K by right-sizing 220 instances, moving batch jobs to spot capacity and adding per-team cost dashboards, with no change in SLO attainment, using AWS and Terraform.

skills.name: Developer Productivity
skills.definition: Shortening the path from commit to production and making other engineers faster and safer.
skills.example: Reduced CI time for a 300-engineer monorepo from 42 to 11 minutes with remote build caching and test sharding, enabling the move from weekly releases to daily deploys, using Bazel.

skills.name: Testing and Code Quality
skills.definition: Keeping defects away from users through tests, review standards and safe rollouts.
skills.example: Built an end-to-end suite for 35 checkout flows run on every pull request, catching 3 to 4 regressions per release and cutting customer-reported checkout bugs 60% in 2 quarters, using Playwright.

skills.name: Data Engineering
skills.definition: Building reliable data movement and processing that products and teams depend on.
metrics: events or records processed per day
skills.example: Replaced nightly batch ETL with a streaming pipeline handling 1.5B events/day, cutting dashboard freshness from 24 hours to under 5 minutes and job failures from ~4 a month to 0, using Spark.

skills.name: Frontend and Mobile
skills.definition: Building fast, accessible client experiences on web or mobile and proving the user-facing effect.
skills.example: Improved product-page LCP from 4.1s to 1.9s and INP from 380ms to 140ms on mobile via code splitting and image streaming, lifting add-to-cart rate 7% in an A/B test, using Next.js.

skills.name: Security and Compliance
skills.definition: Reducing security risk and meeting compliance requirements without slowing delivery.
metrics: vulnerabilities remediated and time to fix
skills.example: Moved secrets for 28 services from config files into a managed vault with automatic rotation, closing 2 audit findings ahead of the company's first SOC 2 Type II, which passed with no exceptions.

skills.name: AI and ML Engineering
skills.definition: Building, evaluating and serving ML or LLM features with measured quality, latency and cost.
metrics: accuracy, precision or recall vs baseline
cost per 1K requests or per task
skills.example: Built a retrieval pipeline and 600-case eval harness for an LLM support bot, raising answer accuracy from 71% to 89% and cutting cost per conversation 45% by routing simple queries to a smaller model.

skills.name: APIs and Integrations
skills.definition: Designing and shipping the interfaces other systems call, and the integrations that connect them.
metrics: calls per day and p99 latency
error rate or 5xx rate before and after
skills.example: Designed a versioned REST API for partner payouts handling 4M calls/day, cutting 5xx rate from 1.8% to 0.2% by adding idempotency keys and per-tenant rate limiting, using Go and Redis.

skills.name: Technical Leadership
skills.definition: Raising other engineers' output through technical direction, design reviews, mentoring and standards.
skills.example: Authored the RFC and led 5 engineers in moving 40 services off a shared database to per-service schemas over 2 quarters, removing the top source of cross-team outages.

examples: teams adopting your design or tool

avoid: Duty statements: Responsible for maintaining backend services
Technology lists with no outcome: Used React, Node.js and AWS
Leading with the tech stack instead of the result
Vanity or effort metrics: lines of code, number of PRs, commits, hours worked
Vague intensifiers: significantly improved, highly scalable, robust, seamless
Numbers you cannot explain or derive in an interview
Claiming you led work you contributed to (led the migration as one of 8 engineers)
Fixed bugs or wrote unit tests as a standalone achievement
Code coverage % as the only quality proof
Internal codenames and undefined acronyms with no context

seniority.entry: Lead with internships, projects and education; show shipped, working code with defensible numbers (users, latency, tests) and name your stack clearly.
seniority.mid: Show ownership of features or services end to end with concrete before/after engineering outcomes; move from implemented to owned, designed and shipped.
seniority.senior: Shift from output to ownership quality: systems you designed, migrations you led, risk you reduced and technical calls a staff engineer could probe for 10 minutes.
seniority.staff_or_lead: Scope is a problem domain, not headcount: RFCs or architecture that changed other teams' roadmaps, org-wide standards and mentorship at scale. Do not claim org-wide strategy you did not own.

structure.bullets_per_role: 3 to 5 for the current role, 2 to 4 for prior roles, 1 to 2 for old or unrelated roles. A few strong bullets beat many average ones.
structure.ordering: Order by relevance to the target role, then by impact; the bullet with the clearest scale or performance number goes first. Early-career resumes add a Projects section ordered by technical depth.
structure.length: One page under about 8 to 10 years. Bullets are 1 to 2 lines; define each acronym once; no paragraphs.
structure.skills_section: Grouped lines on page one: Languages | Frameworks | Data stores | Cloud and infra | Tools. List only what you could be interviewed on, and match the posting's exact terms where true.
structure.summary: Usually omit for new grads. Experienced engineers can use one line on specialty, years, scale and core stack. Education goes first for new grads or under about 3 years.

story_types.name: Performance Win
story_types.proves: Finds and fixes bottlenecks with measurement.
story_types.example: Cut report generation from 90s to 6s for 8K daily users by moving aggregations into materialized views and streaming exports, using PostgreSQL.

story_types.name: Scaling Under Growth
story_types.proves: Keeps systems working as load multiplies.
story_types.example: Sharded the notifications service into 16 partitions ahead of a 5x traffic launch, sustaining 60K messages/sec at p99 under 120ms, using Kafka and Go.

story_types.name: Incident and Hardening
story_types.proves: Handles production pressure and prevents recurrence.
story_types.example: Led mitigation of a 3-hour checkout outage caused by connection pool exhaustion, then added load shedding and saturation alerts; no repeat in the following 9 months.

story_types.name: Safe Migration
story_types.proves: Can change critical systems without breaking them.
story_types.example: Migrated 120M user records from MySQL to PostgreSQL using dual writes and shadow reads, completing cutover with zero downtime and no data loss.

story_types.name: Cost Reduction
story_types.proves: Engineering judgment with business awareness.
story_types.example: Reduced log storage costs $180K a year with tiered retention and sampling of debug logs, keeping all data needed for incident response.

story_types.name: Velocity Multiplier
story_types.proves: Makes other engineers faster.
story_types.example: Built per-pull-request preview environments, cutting QA wait from 1 day to 15 minutes for 80 engineers, using Kubernetes and GitHub Actions.

story_types.name: Zero-to-One Service
story_types.proves: Can design and ship a new system end to end.
story_types.example: Designed and shipped a usage-metering service from scratch that bills 3,000 customers accurate to the cent, enabling the company's first usage-based plan.

story_types.name: Quality Gate
story_types.proves: Raises the quality bar systematically, not one bug at a time.
story_types.example: Introduced canary releases with automatic rollback on error-rate spikes, lowering change failure rate from 12% to 4% across 25 services.

story_types.name: AI or ML in Production
story_types.proves: Ships ML or LLM features with evaluation, latency and cost discipline.
story_types.example: Deployed a fraud-scoring model serving 2K predictions/sec at 30ms p99, catching 18% more fraud at the same false-positive rate, using PyTorch.

story_types.name: Leading Through Others
story_types.proves: Technical influence beyond your own code.
story_types.example: Wrote the API versioning standard and reviewed designs for 6 teams adopting it, cutting breaking-change incidents with mobile clients from 9 a year to 1.

rewrites.weak: Responsible for maintaining backend services in Java.
rewrites.strong: Owned 4 order-management services handling 25M requests/day, cutting p99 latency from 900ms to 240ms by batching database reads, using Java and PostgreSQL.
rewrites.move: Duty to ownership plus a measured outcome; technologies moved to the end.

rewrites.weak: Used React, Redux, Node.js and AWS to build a dashboard.
rewrites.strong: Built a real-time fleet dashboard used daily by 1,200 dispatchers, replacing 30-second polling with sub-second live updates, using React, Node.js and WebSockets.
rewrites.move: Led with what was built and for whom; the stack follows the result.

rewrites.weak: Significantly improved application performance.
rewrites.strong: Reduced checkout page load from 4.6s to 1.8s by code splitting and deferring third-party scripts, raising mobile conversion 6% in a 2-week A/B test.
rewrites.move: Vague intensifier to before/after numbers, the method and the user effect.

rewrites.weak: Wrote unit tests and increased code coverage to 85%.
rewrites.strong: Added contract tests between 6 payment services, catching 11 breaking API changes before release in 2 quarters and cutting payment rollbacks from 5 to 1.
rewrites.move: Proxy metric (coverage) to defect outcomes.

rewrites.weak: Led the migration to Kubernetes.
rewrites.strong: Migrated 14 of the team's 30 services to Kubernetes and wrote the rollout runbook the rest of the team followed, cutting deploy time from 25 to 6 minutes.
rewrites.move: Honest credit: stated your share precisely, then the outcome.

rewrites.weak: Used GitHub Copilot to increase productivity by 50%.
rewrites.strong: Built an LLM-assisted codemod with human review that converted 1,900 legacy test files to the new framework in 3 weeks vs an estimated 4 months.
rewrites.move: Unverifiable productivity claim to a concrete AI-assisted deliverable with scope, control and time saved.

questions.q: Why do you want to join [company]'s engineering team?
Which of our technical challenges or products interests you most, and why?
Describe the most technically challenging project you have worked on and your specific contribution.
Tell us about a production incident you handled: detection, mitigation, root cause and follow-up.
Describe a system you designed. What trade-offs did you make, and what would you change now?
Tell us about a time you significantly improved performance, reliability or cost. How did you measure it?
Share a link to code or a project you are proud of and explain your part in it.
Describe a technical disagreement with a teammate and how it was resolved.
Tell us about a time you shipped under a tight deadline. What did you cut or defer?
How have you helped other engineers grow or raised your team's engineering standards?
How do you use AI coding assistants in your work, and how do you verify their output?
Describe an ML or LLM feature you built or integrated. How did you evaluate quality, latency and cost?

review_notes: Rejected the [verb] + [what you built] + [tech stack] + [result] order from the ex-Amazon guide. Result comes before technologies, which go last, consistent with Orosz and the requirement that impact is readable in a 6-second scan.
Updated frontend metrics: Interaction to Next Paint (INP) replaced First Input Delay as a Core Web Vital in March 2024. Use LCP, INP and CLS; FID bullets read as dated.
Updated accessibility references from WCAG 2.1 to WCAG 2.2 (W3C Recommendation, October 2023); 2.1 AA is still acceptable when a contract or law names it.
Updated DORA delivery metrics: MTTR is now framed as failed deployment recovery time, change failure rate was missing from the notes, and recent DORA reports add rework rate.
Demoted code coverage % and PR or commit counts from outcome metrics to supporting context. They are proxies or effort signals; escaped defects and change failure rate are stronger.
Flagged mentoring bullets that credit promotions (mentored 3 juniors, all promoted) as risky. Promotions have many causes; claim what you did and outcomes you can defend.
Added AI and ML Engineering as a skill with eval-based metrics, plus AI-assisted coding questions. Generic claims like used Copilot to boost productivity 50% are listed as a weak pattern.
Made the role-opening scope line from Tech Interview Handbook optional. It costs a line per role and helps mainly senior or ambiguous titles.
Kept SWE metrics separate from PM: adoption or conversion appears only as the downstream effect of an engineering change, never as the lead.
swe.prompt_rules: SWE bullets. Formula: [engineering outcome, before to after] [at scale] by [technical change the candidate made], using [technologies]. Lead with the result or a strong build verb (cut, scaled, built, migrated, hardened), never with the stack. Metrics that count: p50/p95/p99 latency, throughput (RPS, events/day), availability and SLOs, incidents, recovery time, deploy frequency, lead time, change failure rate, CI time, escaped defects, cloud cost, LCP/INP/CLS, crash-free rate, model accuracy or eval pass rate vs baseline. Include scale (traffic, data, users, services) where real. User or revenue effect may follow as a second clause. Technologies go at the end (using X and Y), at most 3, and only ones the candidate used. State the candidate's share honestly; do not turn contributed into led. Past tense for past work; present tense only for ongoing current-role work. One sentence, 1 to 2 lines, under 230 characters, no first-person pronouns. Never invent numbers; if a number is missing write a [bracketed placeholder] such as [X ms] or [N requests/day]. Banned: responsible for, worked on, helped, assisted, various, significantly, robust, seamless, cutting-edge, lines of code, number of PRs or commits, code coverage as the only result. No em dashes.

bizops.label: Business Operations
bizops.headline: Reviewers scan first for analysis that changed a business decision, the dollars or efficiency it produced, and proof you both planned the work and executed it.
bizops.summary_formula: [Background, e.g. ex-consultant or finance analyst] with [N years] in [domain or sub-function, e.g. GTM strategy, marketplace ops] who turns [type of analysis] into [type of result]; [one signature result in $ or % or a placeholder]. Translate non-strategy experience into strategy and operations language.

bullet_formulas.name: Mini-Case
bullet_formulas.template: [Analyzed what, at what scale] to find [insight], recommended [action] to [decision maker], [business result in $ or %].
bullet_formulas.when: Default for strategy, analytics and recommendation work; reads like a case: problem, analysis, recommendation, result.

bullet_formulas.name: Input and Output
bullet_formulas.template: [Led or ran program] across [input scale: teams, markets, contracts, $ spend], delivering [output: savings, revenue, cycle time] in [timeframe].
bullet_formulas.when: Programs and operational execution where both effort scale and result matter.

bullet_formulas.name: Build the Machine
bullet_formulas.template: Built [model, process, cadence or dashboard] used by [audience] to [decision it drives], cutting [time, error or cost] from [X] to [Y].
bullet_formulas.when: Models, planning processes, KPI systems and automation; must name the decision it powers.

bullet_formulas.name: Identified and Captured
bullet_formulas.template: Identified [$ opportunity] through [analysis], then [action you led with whom] to capture [$ realized] within [timeframe].
bullet_formulas.when: Cost savings and revenue recovery; separates identified from realized dollars.

skills.name: Financial Modeling
skills.definition: Building the model that sizes one decision in dollars and shows which assumptions move the answer.
metrics: budget or plan the model supported
skills.example: Built a driver-based unit economics model for 3 delivery tiers showing same-day orders lost $1.40 each; the CFO-approved repricing lifted contribution margin from 8% to 13% in 2 quarters.

skills.name: Business Case Development
skills.definition: Turning an ambiguous opportunity into a written recommendation with costs, benefits, risks and a clear ask.
skills.example: Built the build-vs-buy case for a customer data platform, recommending a $420K/yr vendor over a 9-engineer internal build; leadership approved and it went live in 4 months vs 14 estimated.

skills.name: Forecasting and Planning
skills.definition: Producing the operating forecast the business plans against, and owning how close it lands.
skills.example: Rebuilt support capacity forecasting around ticket drivers by product line, cutting monthly forecast error from 22% to 7% and avoiding 14 planned hires, about $1.1M in annual cost.

skills.name: Cost Optimization
skills.definition: Finding and capturing cost reductions with an analysis behind each dollar.
metrics: cost per unit, order or ticket
skills.example: Found $2.1M in annual SaaS overlap through a spend analysis of 380 contracts, then led consolidation with IT and procurement to capture $1.6M in savings within 2 quarters.

skills.name: Process Optimization
skills.definition: Redesigning or automating workflows so work gets done faster, cheaper or with fewer errors.
skills.example: Redesigned vendor onboarding from 11 manual handoffs to a 4-step automated workflow, cutting median cycle time from 19 days to 6 and freeing about 120 analyst hours per month.

skills.name: GTM and Revenue Ops
skills.definition: Improving how sales, marketing and customer success turn pipeline into revenue.
skills.example: Rebalanced territories for 45 account executives using account potential scores, raising the share of reps at 80%+ of quota from 52% to 68% and new bookings 14% year over year.

skills.name: KPIs and Operating Cadence
skills.definition: Defining the metrics and review rhythm leaders use to run the business.
metrics: decisions or actions traced to reviews
skills.example: Instituted a weekly business review of 12 KPIs across ops, finance and sales, replacing 9 ad hoc reports; it surfaced a refund spike that led to a policy fix saving $380K a year.

skills.name: Business Analysis and SQL
skills.definition: Pulling the data yourself to answer a business question and settle a decision, rather than to build reporting.
metrics: $ impact of the root cause found
skills.example: Diagnosed a 9-point gross margin drop by querying 2 years of order data in SQL, isolating it to 3 SKUs with mispriced freight; the pricing fix recovered $640K in annualized margin.

skills.name: Strategic Planning
skills.definition: Shaping which bets the company or unit makes over the coming year, with leadership, before any single case is built.
metrics: budget or org size in scope
skills.example: Ran FY26 planning for a 600-person business unit, consolidating 31 team proposals into 8 funded priorities and reallocating $4.5M from low-return projects, approved by the exec team.

skills.name: Market Expansion
skills.definition: Evaluating and launching new markets, segments, channels or partnerships.
skills.example: Sized and ranked 40 metro markets on demand, supply and regulatory cost, then led launch of the top 6 with ops and marketing, reaching $3.2M annualized revenue within 9 months.

skills.name: Program Management
skills.definition: Running a multi-team initiative to completion with owners, milestones and a date that holds.
skills.example: Led a 7-team program moving 2,400 customers to new billing terms before a price change, finishing 3 weeks early with 1.2% churn vs 4% modeled and protecting about $2.8M in ARR.

skills.name: Vendor Management
skills.definition: Selecting, negotiating and managing outside partners against cost, quality and service levels.
skills.example: Ran an RFP across 5 support outsourcing vendors and negotiated per-ticket pricing, cutting cost per ticket from $6.80 to $4.90 while raising CSAT SLA attainment from 88% to 95%.

examples: cost per unit, order or ticket
teams or stakeholders in a program

avoid: Duty statements: Responsible for operations, Owned weekly reporting
Created dashboards for leadership, with no decision or result
Tool lists as the achievement: Proficient in SQL, Tableau and Excel
Analysis with no decision or result: Conducted market analysis
Savings identified presented as savings realized
Input scale with no outcome, or an outcome with no scale
Consulting filler: drove synergies, value-add, best-in-class, holistic
Strategy-only bullets with no execution, or execution with no reasoning
Dense multi-line bullets that bury the number
First-person pronouns and objective statements

seniority.entry: Prove analytical horsepower and execution: models, SQL deep dives and process fixes with measured results; translate consulting, banking or finance work into business-decision language.
seniority.mid: Own initiatives end to end: the recommendation you made, the cross-functional rollout you drove, and the dollars or efficiency realized.
seniority.senior: Show you set the agenda: planning processes, multi-quarter programs, executive alignment, portfolio-level savings or growth, and leadership of analysts.
seniority.staff_or_lead: Show company-level strategy and operating systems: planning and KPI mechanisms the company runs on, influence over a P&L or major budget, and building the BizOps function itself.

structure.bullets_per_role: 3 to 5 for the current role, 2 to 3 for older roles. Former consultants can group bullets by theme or engagement type rather than listing every client.
structure.ordering: Lead with the largest dollar or decision impact. Balance strategic bullets (recommendation, planning) with operational ones (rollout, process) so both show. Mirror the posting's sub-function: GTM, finance, product or customer ops.
structure.length: One page under about 10 years. 1 to 2 lines per bullet, and every bullet contains a number or a placeholder.
structure.skills_section: Specific analytical toolkit: SQL, spreadsheet modeling, Python, a BI tool (Tableau or Looker), CRM (Salesforce); methods such as financial modeling, forecasting and experiment or causal analysis. List certifications only if the posting asks.
structure.summary: Optional 1 to 2 lines: background, domain and one signature result. Most useful for career switchers translating experience into strategy and operations language.

questions.q: Why Business Operations or Strategy & Operations at [company] specifically?

review_notes: Page length: the notes allowed 1 to 2 pages. Corrected to one page under about 10 years, which matches consulting and banking norms that most S&O screeners come from.
Demoted certifications (PMP, Lean Six Sigma). They rarely affect tech BizOps or S&O screens and matter more in manufacturing or logistics operations management.
Updated Sales Ops terminology to RevOps and GTM operations, which is how most current tech postings phrase it.
Dashboards are not outcomes. The notes suggested pairing dashboards with a % performance improvement; the spec requires naming the decision the dashboard drives and its result.
Defined forecast accuracy precisely as forecast error (MAPE) or variance to plan, before and after, instead of an undefined accuracy %.
Added an identified vs realized savings rule. Screeners discount identified-only savings, and the notes' examples mixed the two.
Kept the input plus output metric pairing from the DoorDash S&O guidance and turned it into a named formula.

Reframed the consulting-background point: the notes implied consulting, banking or PE is near-required. Operators and analysts from other paths get hired too when bullets read as mini-cases, so the spec focuses on translation, not pedigree.

Recalibrated seniority to tech S&O levels (analyst or associate, manager, senior manager, director or head). The $60M division, 120-person example is general operations management, not typical tech BizOps scope.
Added AI in Operations as a story type and two AI questions; the notes did not cover AI for this field.
bizops.prompt_rules: BizOps bullets. Formula (mini-case): [analysis done, at what scale] to find [insight], [recommendation or action and who decided], [business result in $ or %]. Lead with the business result or the analytical action; the reader must see the decision the work drove. Pair an input metric (spend analyzed, markets, contracts, teams, stakeholders) with an output metric (annualized savings realized, revenue or bookings, margin, cycle time, hours saved, forecast error, SLA attainment, ROI or payback). Write realized vs identified savings accurately. Show both strategy and execution across the bullets. Tools (SQL, Excel, Tableau, Salesforce) appear only as the means, near the end, never as the achievement. Dashboards, models and reports must name the decision they enabled. Past tense for past work; present tense only for ongoing current-role work. One sentence, 1 to 2 lines, under 230 characters, no first-person pronouns. Never invent numbers; if a number is missing write a [bracketed placeholder] such as [$X] or [N markets]. Banned: responsible for, helped, assisted, supported, worked on, drove synergies, value-add, best-in-class, holistic, various, leveraged, created dashboards for leadership. No em dashes.

data.label: Data Analytics
data.headline: Reviewers scan first for the decision your analysis changed, the data you worked in (scale, sources, messiness), and whether your SQL and BI stack matches theirs.
data.summary_formula: [Data analyst] with [N years] in [domain, e.g. growth, marketplace or finance ops] who [signature pattern, e.g. turns ambiguous questions into decisions leaders act on]; [one proof point with a number or placeholder]. Core stack: [3 to 5 tools from the posting you actually use].

bullet_formulas.name: Question to Decision
bullet_formulas.template: [Analysis you ran] across [data and scale] showed [finding], leading [who] to [decision], which [result].
bullet_formulas.when: Default. The strongest analyst bullet names the decision the analysis changed, not the chart that was produced.

bullet_formulas.name: Metric Moved
bullet_formulas.template: [Moved metric] from [baseline] to [result] by [what your analysis identified and what changed because of it], using [tools].
bullet_formulas.when: When the analysis led to a change you can attribute a number to.

bullet_formulas.name: Self-Serve Reporting
bullet_formulas.template: Built [dashboard or model] covering [scope] for [audience], replacing [manual process] and [adoption or hours saved].
bullet_formulas.when: Dashboard and reporting work. Adoption or time saved is the proof, never the existence of the dashboard.

bullet_formulas.name: Trust in the Numbers
bullet_formulas.template: [Found or fixed data problem] across [tables, sources or scope], cutting [errors, reconciliation time or disputes] from [before] to [after].
bullet_formulas.when: Data quality, instrumentation and governance work, which is usually undersold.

skills.name: SQL and Query Craft
skills.definition: Writing the queries that answer the question, over data big or awkward enough that how you write them matters.
metrics: warehouse credits or cost per run
queries or extracts replaced by one model
skills.example: Rewrote the retention query behind the weekly exec report using window functions, cutting runtime from 14 minutes to 40 seconds across 180M events in Snowflake.

skills.name: Data Modeling and Transformation
skills.definition: Turning raw tables into modeled, tested datasets other people can trust and reuse.
skills.example: Built 22 dbt models with tests behind the growth mart, replacing 9 analysts' one-off queries with one source of truth and cutting dashboard build time from 3 days to half a day.

skills.name: Dashboarding and Self-Serve BI
skills.definition: Building reporting people actually use without asking you for a pull.
metrics: weekly active viewers of the dashboard
ad hoc requests removed per week
time to answer a routine question
skills.example: Shipped a Looker board covering acquisition, activation and churn for 40 weekly users across sales and support, removing about 15 ad hoc data requests a week.

skills.name: Metric Definition and Governance
skills.definition: Deciding what a number means company-wide and making that definition stick.
skills.example: Defined one active-customer metric with finance and sales after an audit found 4 conflicting versions, ending a recurring board-reporting dispute and cutting monthly reconciliation from 6 hours to 30 minutes.

skills.name: Experiment Design and Analysis
skills.definition: Designing tests that can answer the question and reading the results honestly, including the null ones.
metrics: lift on the primary metric with confidence
ship or kill decisions made on the readout
skills.example: Designed and read out 18 pricing experiments with pre-registered power analysis, recommending 5 ships and 13 kills and keeping an apparent 4% lift from shipping once it failed significance.

skills.name: Funnel and Cohort Analysis
skills.definition: Finding where users drop off and how behaviour differs between groups over time.
metrics: cohort retention at D7, D30 or D90
conversion rate change after the fix
skills.example: Traced a 38% checkout drop-off to one address-validation step for international cohorts, a fix that lifted completed orders 9% in the affected markets.

skills.name: Forecasting and Time Series
skills.definition: Projecting a series forward with a method you can defend, and owning how close it lands.
skills.example: Rebuilt the weekly demand forecast with seasonality and promo flags, cutting MAPE from 22% to 9% and letting ops plan staffing 3 weeks out instead of 1.

skills.name: Data Quality and Validation
skills.definition: Making the numbers right, and provably right, before anyone acts on them.
metrics: duplicate or null rate before and after
freshness or SLA on key tables
skills.example: Added freshness and uniqueness tests across 30 source tables, catching a duplicated-orders bug that had overstated revenue reporting by 4% for two weeks.

skills.name: Statistical Analysis in Python or R
skills.definition: Going past SQL when the question needs real statistics or scripted analysis.
skills.example: Modeled churn drivers in Python across 240K accounts, ranking contract length and support-ticket volume above price and redirecting the retention program to the top two.

skills.name: Warehouse Performance and Cost
skills.definition: Keeping the queries, models and extracts analysts depend on fast and affordable.
skills.example: Cut Snowflake spend 31% ($4.2K/month) by partitioning two event tables, switching 6 models to incremental refresh and killing 11 unused scheduled extracts.

skills.name: Stakeholder Readouts and Storytelling
skills.definition: Getting a non-technical audience to the finding and its consequence without walking them through the query.
metrics: audience or seniority of the readout
skills.example: Presented the weekly growth readout to the exec team for 14 months, turning a standing status update into a decision forum that reprioritized spend twice.

skills.name: Revenue and Marketing Analytics
skills.definition: Measuring where revenue comes from, what it costs to get and what it is worth.
skills.example: Built first-touch and multi-touch attribution across 7 channels, showing paid social payback at 19 months and shifting $600K of annual spend to referral and lifecycle.

examples: ship or kill calls made on a readout
revenue or margin influenced (state attribution honestly)
query or refresh runtime before and after
time to answer a routine question
ad hoc requests removed per week

avoid: Tool lists as achievements: Used SQL, Tableau and Excel daily
Dashboard counting: Built 15 dashboards, with no audience or use
Responsible for reporting, Assisted with analysis, Supported the team with data
Analyzed large datasets with no scale, source or finding named
Gathered requirements and delivered insights, with no decision attached
Claiming revenue you only reported on; say what your analysis changed
Generated reports, which describes the output and not the result
Data-driven, actionable insights, deep dive and leveraged as filler
Significance claimed without a test, or percentages with no baseline
Padding with coursework-level projects once you have real experience

seniority.entry: Lead with projects, internships and coursework that used real data; name the dataset, its size and the question, and show one finding someone acted on. SQL and one BI tool beat a long tool list.
seniority.mid: Show ownership of a reporting area or domain end to end: the models you built, the stakeholders you served, and decisions that moved because of your analysis.
seniority.senior: Shift from answering questions to setting them: metric definitions others adopted, experiment standards, and analyses that changed a roadmap or a budget rather than a slide.
seniority.lead: Scope is a domain and a set of standards, not headcount: the data model other analysts build on, the governance that ended an argument, and the exec forum you own. Do not claim data-engineering ownership you did not have.

structure.bullets_per_role: 3 to 5 for the current role, 2 to 4 for prior roles, 1 to 2 for old or unrelated roles. Lead each role with the bullet whose decision is biggest.
structure.ordering: Order by relevance to the posting, then by the size of the decision. The bullet with the clearest business consequence goes first, not the one with the fanciest method.
structure.length: One page under about 8 to 10 years. Bullets are 1 to 2 lines. Spell out a metric once before abbreviating it.
structure.skills_section: Grouped on page one: Languages and querying | Warehouses | BI and visualization | Statistics and methods. Match the posting's exact tool names where true, and list only what you could be interviewed on.
structure.summary: One line on domain, years, the kind of decisions you support and your core stack. Education first for new grads or under about 3 years, especially for quantitative degrees.

review_notes: Separated this vertical from Business Operations deliberately. Bizops keeps Business Analysis and SQL, which is analysis in service of a business decision; this vertical covers the analyst craft itself, including modeling, governance and experiment design.

Kept Data Modeling and Transformation distinct from the Software Engineering guide's Data Engineering: this is modeling inside the warehouse for analysis, not building the pipelines and platforms that move data.
Led the skill set with SQL rather than Python. Postings reviewed treat advanced SQL plus one BI tool as the required floor and Python or R as the differentiator, so ordering follows that.
Made the decision, not the dashboard, the unit of achievement in bullet_formulas and avoid. The most common weak analyst bullet names an artifact with no audience and no consequence.
Included Data Quality and Validation as a first-class skill because it is routinely undersold on analyst resumes and routinely probed in interviews.
Included Warehouse Performance and Cost because cloud spend now sits with analysts as often as with platform teams.
Experiment guidance requires power or significance before a lift is claimed, and treats a kill as a positive result, to keep the app from inviting invented wins.
data.prompt_rules: Data analytics bullets. Formula: [analysis you ran] across [data and scale] showed [finding], leading to [decision or change], which [result]. Lead with the decision or the moved number, never with the tool. Metrics that count: decisions changed, spend or headcount reallocated, revenue or cost influenced (state attribution honestly), conversion or retention moved, forecast accuracy or MAPE, experiment lift with confidence, rows or events analyzed, sources joined, dashboard weekly viewers, ad hoc requests removed, query or refresh runtime, warehouse cost, data issues caught before release. Name the data's scale or messiness where real. Tools go at the end (using X and Y), at most 3, and only ones the candidate used. A dashboard, report or model is not an achievement on its own: say who used it and what changed. Treat a kill or a null result as a legitimate outcome. Never claim significance without a test, or a percentage without a baseline. State the candidate's share honestly; do not turn supported into led. Past tense for past work; present tense only for ongoing current-role work. One sentence, 1 to 2 lines, under 230 characters, no first-person pronouns. Never invent numbers; if a number is missing write a [bracketed placeholder] such as [N rows] or [X% accuracy]. Banned: responsible for, assisted with, various, actionable insights, data-driven, deep dive, leveraged, robust, seamless, large datasets with no size, number of dashboards as the only result. No em dashes.
